newsitem.title: CHINA: China car market stalling, inventories rise.
newsitem.headline: China car market stalling, inventories rise.

text.p: China's car market is in the doldrums because of overproduction, fierce competition, poor roads and local protectionism, the official media and salesmen said on Thursday.

"We have 15,000 cars in stock, higher than the usual level," said a salesman for Shanghai Automobile Industry Group (SAIG) which sells China's top passenger car, the Santana. Output of the Santana, a joint venture with Germany's Volkswagen AG, is due to reach 200,000 this year, up from 160,000 in 1995.

"The inventory situation of other manufacturers is worse than ours," he said. "The domestic market is weak because of oversupply, too many imports, protectionism by local governments aimed at keeping out Santanas and a chaotic market."
In 1995, China produced 1.5 million vehicles, up 10 percent from 1994. It is expected to produce 2.7 million in 2000.
China's vehicle output in the first half of 1996 was 758,000, official figures show.
The Shanghai-based Business News said China's auto industry suffered badly in the first half of 1996, with serious losses in June and July.
It blamed an excess of imported cars, a serious shortage of roads, the negative impact of the auto industry on the environment and a shortage of capital.
It called for a standardised, transparent and reasonable tax system to replace the current "chaotic" system that discouraged people from buying cars.
Buyers are now confronted by different prices for the same car in different cities and towns.

The SAIG salesman said that some provinces and cities were limiting sales of Santanas by branding them "corrupt cars". They also were refusing to issue licences for them, arguing the Santana was not 100 percent Chinese. The salesman said the car had a Chinese content of more than 95 percent.

Yang Sheng, an official of the Shanghai Shenshi Motors Centre, said an austerity policy launched in July 1993 was a major factor in the downturn, because it had limited credit and restricted purchases by state companies.
"Car output in China is higher than demand," Yang said. "I see a gradual easing of the policy which will push up demand. This weakness in the market is temporary."
"Like South Korea, we should protect our domestic manufacturers and gradually reduce car imports," he said.

In the first half of 1996, China legally imported 35,700 cars, down 30 percent from the same 1995 period. But thousands more are smuggled in to satisfy demand from the rich and powerful for imported models such as Cadillacs, Lexus and Mercedes.
Another sales disincentive is charges by local governments wanting to limit the number of cars on overcrowded roads.

Shanghai auctions car licences, with prices up to 150,000 yuan ($18,072), equal to the cost of a new Santana. Other cities charge fees of up to 20 percent of the price of the car, industry officials said.
